title: Asymmetric ideological segregation in exposure to political news on Facebook
screen_reason: No quantitative share of misinformation with a denominator is reported anywhere in this text. The paper measures ideological SEGREGATION of political-news exposure on Facebook (a segregation index of about 0.35 for domains and 0.45-0.50 for URLs) and the ideological leaning of audiences. Its two misinformation numbers - '71, 76, and 76% of untrustworthy domains have audiences that are conservative on average' and '97% of false URLs in each case have audiences that are conservative on average' - have untrustworthy domains / false URLs as their DENOMINATOR and conservative-leaning audience as their numerator. They describe who consumes misinformation, not what share of content, exposure or sharing is misinformation, so they satisfy none of the six eligible constructs. The one place the paper speaks to prevalence it does so only qualitatively: 'Only a small fraction of all domains is classified as untrustworthy; the fraction of false news stories is barely perceptible because it is very small compared with the full volume of news stories.' FLAG FOR ADJUDICATION: this is a screening call made on the main text alone. The numbers that would make this paper eligible are almost certainly in the supplementary materials (SM sections S4.1 and S6, and the underlying data behind Figs. 1C, 1D and 4), which are not part of this file. If the SM is available to the review, this paper very plausibly becomes INCLUDE.
missed_or_uncertain: Everything misinformation-related that I saw and why no row was created. (1) Fig. 3A caption: 'For potential, exposed, and engaged audiences, 71, 76, and 76% of untrustworthy domains have audiences that are conservative on average (favorability score > 0).' Denominator = untrustworthy domains; numerator = those with a conservative-leaning audience. This is the ideological composition of misinformation AUDIENCES, not a prevalence of misinformation, so it fits none of RECALL/CONTENT/EXPOSURE/REACH/SHARING/CONCENTRATION. (2) Fig. 3C caption: 'For potential, exposed, and engaged audiences, 97% of false URLs in each case have audiences that are conservative on average.' Same structure, same reason. (3) Fig. 4 color-codes the '% untrustworthy domains' and '% unreliable URLs' within the top three coexposure communities; the only numbers reachable in this text are the legend scale ticks (0.05 and 0.10 for untrustworthy domains; 0.0025, 0.0050, 0.0075 for unreliable URLs). Those are axis breakpoints on a continuous colour scale, not a stated estimate for any named community, so no value can be extracted under R8. They do indicate the order of magnitude: roughly 5-10% of domains in a community untrustworthy, and roughly 0.25-0.75% of URLs rated false. (4) Figs. 1C and 1D plot daily counts of untrustworthy vs trustworthy domains and false vs not-rated-false URLs, but no counts appear in the text; the totals given are only the corpus sizes (about 35,000 unique domains and about 640,000 unique URLs shared more than 100 times, for about 208 million US adult active users). A prevalence would be immediately derivable if the untrustworthy/false counts were stated - they are not. (5) 'posts classified as political news that contain a URL ... amount to about 3% of all posts shared by US adult users and 3.9% of all content that US adult users saw on the platform during our study period' - the share of POLITICAL NEWS, not of misinformation, so not eligible. (6) The segregation index (about 0.35 for domains, 0.45-0.50 for URLs, 'three times as high as a web-tracking benchmark for the same set of individuals') and the favorability scores are index values, not shares of misinformation. (7) 'Gentzkow and Shapiro (5) ... found a gap of exposure to conservatives between conservatives and liberals of 7.5 percentage points (60.6% for conservatives and 53.1% for liberals)' is a figure the paper cites from elsewhere and concerns conservative content, not misinformation; R8 bars it twice over. (8) 'pjmedia.com published the most-viewed story during the observation period ... viewed 113,272,405 times' is a raw view count with no denominator, and the story is not stated to be rated false. (9) 'users classified as having high political interest are twice as segregated as low-interest users' and 'Pages and Groups contribute much more to segregation and audience polarization than users' are SM findings reported as ratios/qualitative comparisons. (10) No CONCENTRATION row is possible: the paper's central claim that 'most misinformation ... exists within this homogeneously conservative corner' is never expressed as a top group's share of users/sources together with their share of exposure, so R1 cannot be met.

rob.design: Platform-internal observational study, part of the US 2020 Facebook and Instagram Election Study (Meta plus external academics; preanalysis plan at https://osf.io/2y84h). Aggregated exposure and engagement metrics for N approximately 208 million US-based adult active Facebook users whose ideology could be predicted by Facebook's internal ideology classifier (out of 231 million active US users in the period), covering all URLs classified as political news by Facebook's internal civic and news classifiers and posted between 1 September 2020 and 1 February 2021: approximately 35,000 unique domains and approximately 640,000 unique URLs. Privacy constraints: no individual-level data, and only URLs shared more than 100 times were analysed. Three audience measures per URL/domain - potential (could have seen), exposed (saw in Feed), engaged (clicked, reacted, liked, reshared or commented). Misinformation ground truth: URLs rated false by Meta's Third-Party Fact-Checking Program as of 15 February 2021, and domains labelled untrustworthy when two or more of their URLs were rated false. Ideology dichotomised at classifier scores <= 0.35 (liberal) and >= 0.65 (conservative). Stated limitations directly relevant to any prevalence use: the 3PFC measure 'likely undercounts the total volume of false news circulating on the platform' because 'only a tiny amount of inventory ever makes it to the 3PFC'; the analysis excludes non-URL platform content; and the results depend on Facebook's proprietary classifiers, which the authors say need robustness testing against alternatives. Substantial Meta funding and Meta co-authorship are disclosed.
rob.item6_quote: News stories are classified as "false" if the URL was rated false by Meta's Third-Party Fact-Checking Program (3PFC) as of 15 February 2021 (SM section S3.4). This measure of "misinformation" likely undercounts the total volume of false news circulating on the platform; but whereas specific false news stories may go undetected (i.e., only a tiny amount of inventory ever makes it to the 3PFC), untrustworthy labels at the domain level, which are applied whenever a domain had two or more URLs rated false by the 3PFC, have better coverage and are more reliable (SM section S4.1).
rob.item10_quote: For potential, exposed, and engaged audiences, 71, 76, and 76% of untrustworthy domains have audiences that are conservative on average (favorability score > 0). ... For potential, exposed, and engaged audiences, 97% of false URLs in each case have audiences that are conservative on average.
